data.title: The Rommel-Pot Player

thumbnail.alt_text: A work made of oil on panel.

data.description: Joy alights on the faces of a crowd of children staring spellbound up at a rommel-pot player. A rommel pot is a musical instrument made out of an earthenware jar with a stick inserted through an animal skin covering. The player rotates and rubs the stick to produce a droning noise akin to a duck call. It was often played during Shrovetide, the festive period before the start of Lent, also known as Carnival. This street performer wears a foxtail hat, a traditional attribute of a fool, highlighting the silliness of the occasion. Frans Hals’s workshop produced multiple versions of this scene, which was likely popular for the way the artist captured childhood delight.

data.provenance_text: Friedrich Jakob Gsell, Vienna, died 1871; his estate sale, Georg Plach, Vienna, 14 March, 1872, no. 38, as Frans Hals for fl. 6,050 to Lützow [according to Frimmel 1914].  Schorer, Berlin, by 1883 [according to Bode 1883]; his sale Groot Bentveld, near Haarlem, April 26-27, 1892, no. 32, for fl. 6,000 to Goedhart [according to annotated catalogue at R.K.D, The Hague, and Hofstede de Groot 1910].  Salomon Goldschmidt Junior, Frankfurt-am-Main, by 1910 [according to Hofstede de Groot 1910]. William J. McAneeny, Detroit, by 1929, died 1935; his widow until 1936 [lent to New York 1929 and Detroit 1935]. Karl Lilienfeld Galleries, New York, by 1936, until 1938 [Lilienfeld shipped the painting to the Art Institute for purchase consideration, April 9, 1936, receipt R 5993, lent it to Haarlem 1937, and sent it to the Art Institute again on September 28, 1938, receipt R 6680 in Registrar’s records]; sold by Lilienfeld to Charles H. Worcester, Chicago, 1938 [Art Institute registrar’s shipping order 27321 shows it was sent to Charles Worcester for purchase consideration in October 1938]; given to the Art Institute, 1947.
